frames.narration: A guest searches for a Deluxe room from the 16th to the 19th of October, which is three nights. The API answers from the availability cache, which is a few seconds old, and shows 'only 2 left'.
The guest clicks Book. The request carries an idempotency key, so a retry will be recognised. The booking service now does the exact check against the real inventory, ignoring the cache.

In one transaction, the service runs a conditional update on each night: add one to 'held' only if sold plus held is below the limit. The limit is 42, which is 40 rooms plus an allowance of 2. The three nights are at 39, 41 and 38, so all three updates succeed.

At the same moment another guest wants the 17th and 18th. The 17th is already at 42 of 42, so that update changes zero rows. The whole transaction rolls back, and the second guest is told the room has gone. Nobody can pass the limit, however many servers run this code.
The guest pays. The payment request carries the same key, so if it is sent twice there is still one charge. The hold is still live, with eight minutes left.

The service turns the hold into a booking: 'held' goes down by one and 'sold' goes up by one on each of the three nights. The total used is unchanged, and the room can no longer expire. If the app had sent the request again, the key k-318 would simply return this booking.

In the same commit the service wrote an event. A relay publishes it, the cache is told to drop the Deluxe entry for those dates, and the channel manager closes the last Deluxe rooms on partner sites. Partners may still show a room for a few seconds, and that is the reason the final check is always on the real inventory.
